questionText: What is C++?
options: A purely functional programming language
A general-purpose, compiled language that extends C with object-oriented and generic programming features
A scripting language that runs inside a browser
A markup language for describing documents
explanation: C++ is a general-purpose programming language created as an extension of C, adding object-oriented, generic, and (later) functional features while keeping low-level memory control and high performance.

questionText: What is the main difference between C and C++?
options: C++ is interpreted while C is compiled
C++ adds object-oriented programming, templates, and the STL on top of C's procedural model
C and C++ are the same language with different file extensions
C++ cannot call C libraries
explanation: C++ was designed as 'C with Classes'. It keeps C's low-level capabilities but adds classes, inheritance, templates, exceptions, and the Standard Template Library.

questionText: What is a pointer in C++?
options: A variable that stores a fixed value
A variable that stores the memory address of another variable
A type of array
A function that returns void
explanation: A pointer holds the memory address of another variable. It is declared using the * symbol, e.g. int* ptr, and can be dereferenced with * to access the value it points to.

questionText: What is a reference in C++?
options: A pointer that can be reassigned freely
An alias for an existing variable that must be initialized when declared and cannot be null
A copy of a variable's value
A keyword used only in templates
explanation: A reference (declared with &) is an alias for an existing object. Unlike a pointer, it must be bound to a valid object at declaration and cannot later refer to a different object or be null.

questionText: What is a key difference between a pointer and a reference?
options: References can be reseated to point elsewhere; pointers cannot
Pointers can be null and reassigned; references must be initialized and always refer to the same object
There is no difference, they are interchangeable in every context
References use more memory than pointers
explanation: Pointers can be null, reassigned, and support pointer arithmetic. References must be bound at initialization, cannot be null, and cannot be made to refer to a different object afterward.

questionText: What does the const keyword do in C++?
options: It marks a variable as thread-local
It indicates that a variable, parameter, or method promises not to modify the value it applies to
It makes a variable global
It allocates memory on the heap
explanation: const declares that a value cannot be modified after initialization. Applied to a member function (e.g. void foo() const), it promises the method will not modify the object's state.

questionText: What does the static keyword mean when applied to a class member in C++?
options: The member can only be used once
The member belongs to the class itself rather than to any single instance, and is shared across all instances
The member is automatically const
The member is stored on the stack instead of the heap
explanation: A static member belongs to the class rather than to individual objects. There is exactly one copy shared by all instances, and it can be accessed without creating an object.

questionText: What is the purpose of a header file (.h / .hpp) in C++?
options: It contains compiled machine code
It declares interfaces (classes, functions, constants) so multiple source files can share them via #include
It stores runtime configuration
It replaces the need for a compiler
explanation: Header files contain declarations (function prototypes, class definitions, constants) that are shared between translation units using #include, separating interface from implementation.

questionText: What are the main stages of building a C++ program?
options: Writing and running only
Preprocessing, compilation, assembly, and linking
Interpretation and garbage collection
Bytecode generation and JIT compilation
explanation: A C++ build pipeline preprocesses source (handling #include/#define), compiles it to assembly, assembles it to object code, then links object files and libraries into an executable.

questionText: What is the standard signature of the main function in C++?
options: void main()
int main() or int main(int argc, char* argv[])
public static void main(String[] args)
def main():
explanation: The C++ standard requires main to return an int, either taking no parameters or taking argc/argv for command-line arguments. Returning 0 conventionally signals success.

questionText: What is the difference between struct and class in C++?
options: struct cannot have member functions
The only difference is the default access level: public for struct, private for class
class cannot be used with templates
struct is only for C compatibility and has no other use
explanation: In C++, struct and class are almost identical; the only difference is default member and inheritance access, which is public for struct and private for class.

questionText: What is function overloading in C++?
options: Calling a function too many times
Defining multiple functions with the same name but different parameter lists
Overriding a virtual function in a derived class
Using too many arguments in a single function
explanation: Function overloading allows multiple functions to share a name as long as their parameter lists differ in number or type, letting the compiler pick the right one at compile time.

questionText: What is a namespace in C++?
options: A block of memory reserved at runtime
A declarative region that provides a scope to group identifiers and avoid naming collisions
A type of template
A synonym for a header file
explanation: A namespace (e.g. namespace std { ... }) groups related identifiers under a named scope, preventing name clashes between libraries or modules.

questionText: What are default parameters in C++?
options: Parameters that are always ignored
Function parameters that are given a default value used when the caller omits an argument
Parameters that must be pointers
Parameters automatically generated by the compiler for every function
explanation: A default parameter (e.g. void greet(std::string name = "World")) supplies a value used automatically when the caller does not provide one, reducing the need for overloads.

questionText: What is the this pointer in C++?
options: A pointer to the parent class
An implicit pointer available in non-static member functions that points to the object the method was called on
A pointer to the first element of an array
A global pointer to the main function
explanation: Inside a non-static member function, this is an implicit pointer to the calling object, used to access its members or to distinguish them from same-named parameters.

questionText: What is Object-Oriented Programming in the context of C++?
options: Programming that only uses objects, never functions
A paradigm organizing code into classes and objects that bundle data with the operations on that data
A style unique to Java that C++ merely imitates
A programming style with no data types
explanation: C++ supports OOP by letting you define classes that bundle data (member variables) with behavior (member functions), enabling encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism.

questionText: What are the four main pillars of OOP in C++?
options: Compilation, Linking, Loading, Execution
Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, Polymorphism
Public, Private, Protected, Static
Stack, Heap, Global, Local
explanation: Encapsulation hides internal state, abstraction exposes only essential details, inheritance lets classes derive from others, and polymorphism lets one interface work with multiple types.

questionText: What is inheritance in C++?
options: Copying a class's code manually into another file
A mechanism where a derived class acquires members and behavior from a base class
A way to import a library
A feature only available for structs, not classes
explanation: Inheritance lets a derived class reuse and extend the members of a base class, expressed with class Derived : public Base { ... } for public inheritance.

questionText: What is polymorphism in C++?
options: Having several variables with the same name
The ability to call the correct derived-class implementation of a function through a base-class pointer or reference
Defining a class with multiple constructors
Using multiple namespaces in one file
explanation: Runtime polymorphism in C++ lets code that holds a base-class pointer or reference invoke the actual derived-class implementation of a virtual function, chosen at runtime.

questionText: What is a virtual function in C++?
options: A function that exists only during debugging
A member function declared in a base class that can be overridden in derived classes and is resolved at runtime via dynamic dispatch
A function that cannot be called directly
A function that runs on a separate thread
explanation: Declaring a base-class method virtual enables dynamic dispatch: calling it through a base pointer/reference invokes the most-derived override, using the object's vtable at runtime.

questionText: What is a pure virtual function and how does it create an abstract class?
options: A virtual function with an empty body that behaves like any normal function
A virtual function declared with = 0, which has no implementation in that class and forces any concrete derived class to override it, making the class abstract
A function that can only be called from main()
A static function that cannot be inherited
explanation: Declaring virtual void foo() = 0; makes foo a pure virtual function. A class with at least one pure virtual function becomes abstract and cannot be instantiated directly.

questionText: What is operator overloading in C++?
options: Using too many operators in one expression
Defining custom behavior for operators (like +, ==, <<) when applied to user-defined types
A compiler error caused by ambiguous operators
Overloading only arithmetic operators is allowed
explanation: C++ allows you to redefine what operators like +, ==, or << do for your own classes, e.g. operator+(const T& other), so objects can be used naturally with familiar syntax.

questionText: What is the diamond problem in C++?
options: A performance issue related to nested loops
An ambiguity that arises with multiple inheritance when a class inherits from two classes that share a common base, causing duplicate base subobjects
A syntax error when using templates
A memory alignment issue with structs
explanation: If classes B and C both inherit from A, and D inherits from both B and C, D ends up with two copies of A's members unless A is inherited virtually (virtual inheritance).

questionText: What is encapsulation in C++?
options: Combining every class into a single file
Bundling data and the methods that operate on it together, restricting direct access to internal state via access specifiers like private
Compiling code into a single binary
Wrapping a function in a try/catch block
explanation: Encapsulation groups data and behavior inside a class and controls access using public, protected, and private specifiers, protecting internal state from unintended external modification.

questionText: What are constructors and destructors in C++?
options: Functions that must be called manually to create and delete objects
Special member functions: a constructor initializes an object when it is created, a destructor (~ClassName) cleans up when it is destroyed
Keywords used only with pointers
Functions that only exist for structs
explanation: A constructor (same name as the class) runs automatically when an object is created to initialize it; a destructor (prefixed with ~) runs automatically when the object goes out of scope or is deleted, freeing resources.

questionText: What is RAII in C++?
options: A naming convention for private members
Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: tying a resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime so it is automatically released when the object is destroyed
A type of runtime exception
A keyword for declaring arrays
explanation: RAII acquires a resource (memory, file handle, lock) in a constructor and releases it in the destructor, so resources are automatically freed when the owning object goes out of scope, even during exceptions.

questionText: What is the difference between new/delete and malloc/free in C++?
options: They are identical and interchangeable in every case
new/delete call constructors and destructors and are type-safe; malloc/free only allocate raw memory without initialization
malloc is faster in all cases so it should always be preferred
delete cannot free memory allocated by new
explanation: new invokes the type's constructor after allocating memory and delete invokes the destructor before freeing it. malloc/free (inherited from C) only manage raw memory and know nothing about object construction.

questionText: What is a memory leak in C++?
options: When a program uses too much CPU
When dynamically allocated memory is never freed, so it remains unreachable but still reserved for the program's lifetime
When a variable is declared but never used
When a file is opened but never read
explanation: A memory leak occurs when memory allocated with new (or malloc) is never released with delete (or free), and no pointer to it remains, so it cannot be reclaimed until the process exits.

questionText: What is a dangling pointer?
options: A pointer that has never been initialized
A pointer that still refers to memory that has already been freed or gone out of scope
A pointer that points to a constant
A pointer used inside a template
explanation: A dangling pointer points to memory that has been deallocated (e.g. after delete) or to a local variable that has gone out of scope. Dereferencing it causes undefined behavior.

questionText: What is std::unique_ptr (C++11)?
options: A pointer that can be shared by multiple owners simultaneously
A smart pointer that exclusively owns a dynamically allocated object and automatically deletes it when it goes out of scope
A raw pointer wrapper with no automatic cleanup
A pointer only usable inside templates
explanation: std::unique_ptr provides exclusive ownership of a heap object; it cannot be copied (only moved) and automatically calls delete on the owned object when the unique_ptr is destroyed.

questionText: What is std::shared_ptr (C++11)?
options: A pointer that must be manually reference-counted by the programmer
A smart pointer that allows multiple owners of the same object via reference counting, deleting it once the last owner is destroyed
A pointer that can never be null
A pointer that only works with arrays
explanation: std::shared_ptr uses an internal reference count so multiple shared_ptr instances can co-own the same object; the object is deleted automatically once the last shared_ptr referencing it is destroyed.

questionText: What is the Rule of Three (and Rule of Five) in C++?
options: A rule limiting classes to three member functions
If a class manages a resource, it should define its own copy constructor, copy assignment operator, and destructor (and, since C++11, also the move constructor and move assignment operator)
A rule about how many times a loop can run
A naming convention for template parameters
explanation: If you must define one of the destructor, copy constructor, or copy assignment operator because a class owns a resource, you generally need all three (Rule of Three); C++11 extends this to five by adding the move constructor and move assignment operator.

questionText: What is the STL in C++?
options: A build tool for compiling C++ programs
The Standard Template Library: a collection of generic containers, iterators, and algorithms
A GUI framework bundled with the compiler
A networking library
explanation: The Standard Template Library (STL) provides generic, reusable containers (vector, map, set...), iterators to traverse them, and algorithms (sort, find, accumulate...) that work across container types.

questionText: What is the difference between std::vector and std::array?
options: They are exactly the same
std::vector is a dynamically resizable array on the heap; std::array is a fixed-size array whose size is known at compile time
std::array can grow at runtime while std::vector cannot
std::vector cannot store primitive types
explanation: std::vector manages a dynamically resizable, heap-allocated array that can grow or shrink at runtime. std::array (C++11) is a fixed-size, stack-allocated array whose size is a compile-time constant.

questionText: What is the difference between std::vector and std::list?
options: They provide identical performance for every operation
std::vector stores elements contiguously (fast random access, slower middle insert/erase); std::list is a doubly-linked list (fast insert/erase anywhere, no random access)
std::list cannot store custom objects
std::vector is always slower than std::list
explanation: std::vector keeps elements in contiguous memory, giving O(1) random access but O(n) insertion/removal in the middle. std::list is a doubly-linked list with O(1) insertion/removal anywhere but only sequential access.

questionText: What is std::map in C++?
options: An unordered hash table with no sorting guarantees
An associative container that stores key-value pairs sorted by key, typically implemented as a balanced binary search tree
A container that can only store strings
A synonym for std::vector
explanation: std::map stores unique keys mapped to values, keeping them sorted by key (usually via a red-black tree), giving O(log n) lookup, insertion, and removal.

questionText: What is an iterator in C++?
options: A function that repeats a loop a fixed number of times
An object that behaves like a pointer, used to traverse elements of a container without exposing its internal representation
A keyword for declaring a for loop
A container that stores only integers
explanation: Iterators provide a uniform, pointer-like interface (operator++, operator*, etc.) for traversing containers, letting STL algorithms work with vectors, lists, maps, and more without knowing their internals.

questionText: What does std::sort do, and where does it live?
options: It is a member function of every container defined in <vector>
It is a generic algorithm in <algorithm> that sorts a range given by two iterators, typically using an introsort-based approach
It only works on arrays of integers
It permanently modifies the type of the container
explanation: std::sort, declared in <algorithm>, sorts elements in the range [first, last) given by iterators, and works with any container offering random-access iterators, such as std::vector.

questionText: What is the difference between std::map and std::unordered_map?
options: There is no meaningful difference
std::map keeps keys sorted using a tree (O(log n) operations); std::unordered_map uses a hash table for average O(1) operations but no ordering
std::unordered_map can only store one element
std::map cannot use custom key types
explanation: std::map maintains keys in sorted order via a balanced tree, giving O(log n) operations. std::unordered_map (C++11) uses a hash table for average O(1) operations but does not maintain any particular order.

questionText: What is std::pair (and std::tuple) used for?
options: Only for storing two numbers
std::pair bundles exactly two values of possibly different types; std::tuple generalizes this to any fixed number of values
They are containers that can grow dynamically like std::vector
They replace the need for structs entirely
explanation: std::pair<T1, T2> groups two heterogeneous values (e.g. map entries are std::pair<Key, Value>). std::tuple extends this idea to an arbitrary fixed number of heterogeneous values.

questionText: What does the auto keyword do in C++11?
options: It marks a variable for automatic garbage collection
It tells the compiler to deduce a variable's type automatically from its initializer
It makes a variable thread-local
It is only usable for function return types before C++14
explanation: auto instructs the compiler to infer the variable's type from its initializer at compile time, e.g. auto x = 5; deduces x as int. It does not mean dynamic typing.

questionText: What is a range-based for loop, introduced in C++11?
options: A loop that can only iterate over arrays of fixed size
A concise for-loop syntax that iterates directly over the elements of a container or array without explicit indices or iterators
A loop that automatically parallelizes across threads
A loop that replaces while loops entirely
explanation: Range-based for loops, written as for (auto& elem : container), iterate over every element of a range (container, array, initializer list) without manually managing indices or iterators.

questionText: What is a lambda expression in C++11?
options: A macro that expands at compile time
An anonymous, inline function object that can capture variables from its enclosing scope
A special kind of class template
A function that can only be called once
explanation: A lambda, e.g. [x](int y) { return x + y; }, defines an unnamed function object inline. The capture list [x] specifies which enclosing variables it can use, by value or reference.

questionText: What is nullptr, introduced in C++11?
options: A macro equal to the integer 0, identical to the old NULL
A type-safe keyword representing a null pointer value, distinct from integer 0, that avoids overload-resolution ambiguity
A pointer that always points to the first element of an array
A reserved variable name that cannot be reassigned
explanation: nullptr has its own type (std::nullptr_t) and unambiguously represents a null pointer, fixing issues where the old NULL macro (often defined as 0) could be confused with an integer in overload resolution.

questionText: What are move semantics and rvalue references (C++11)?
options: A way to physically relocate objects in memory automatically
A mechanism (using && rvalue references) that lets resources be transferred from a temporary or expiring object instead of deep-copied, improving performance
A restriction preventing objects from being copied at all
A feature exclusive to primitive types like int and double
explanation: Rvalue references (T&&) let code detect temporary (movable) objects and 'steal' their internal resources via a move constructor/assignment instead of performing an expensive deep copy.

questionText: What are variadic templates in C++11?
options: Templates that can only accept exactly two type parameters
Templates that accept an arbitrary number of template arguments of possibly different types
A way to define templates without any parameters
Templates restricted to numeric types only
explanation: Variadic templates, using a parameter pack (typename... Args), let a template function or class accept any number of arguments of varying types, enabling things like a type-safe printf replacement.

questionText: What is an enum class (scoped enumeration) in C++11?
options: An enum whose values can implicitly convert to int and pollute the surrounding scope
A strongly-typed enumeration whose enumerators are scoped to the enum's name and do not implicitly convert to int
A class that behaves exactly like a plain enum
An enum that can only hold string values
explanation: enum class Color { Red, Green }; requires Color::Red to access enumerators, and disallows implicit conversion to int, avoiding the naming collisions and unsafe conversions of plain C-style enums.

questionText: What are generic lambdas, introduced in C++14?
options: Lambdas that can never capture variables
Lambdas whose parameters can be declared auto, letting a single lambda work with multiple argument types like a template
Lambdas that must specify every type explicitly
A feature that lets lambdas be recursive by default
explanation: C++14 allows lambda parameters to be declared auto, e.g. [](auto a, auto b) { return a + b; }, making the lambda's operator() effectively a template that works with any compatible types.

questionText: What does std::make_unique do, added in C++14?
options: It creates a std::shared_ptr
It safely constructs an object and wraps it in a std::unique_ptr in a single, exception-safe expression
It converts a raw pointer into a reference
It duplicates an existing unique_ptr
explanation: std::make_unique<T>(args...) allocates and constructs a T and returns it owned by a std::unique_ptr, avoiding manual new calls and certain exception-safety pitfalls. (std::make_shared existed since C++11.)

questionText: What changed with constexpr functions in C++14?
options: constexpr functions were removed entirely
Restrictions were relaxed so constexpr functions could contain loops, local variables, and multiple statements, not just a single return expression
constexpr became the default for every function
constexpr functions can now throw exceptions at compile time
explanation: C++11 constexpr functions were limited to essentially a single return statement. C++14 relaxed this, allowing loops, conditionals, and multiple local variables inside constexpr functions.

questionText: What are structured bindings, introduced in C++17?
options: A way to bind a function to a specific thread
Syntax that lets you unpack multiple values from a pair, tuple, struct, or array into individually named variables in one declaration
A feature restricted to arrays of exactly three elements
A replacement for the auto keyword
explanation: Structured bindings, e.g. auto [key, value] = *mapIterator;, let you destructure a pair, tuple, struct, or array into named variables in a single statement.

questionText: What is std::optional, introduced in C++17?
options: A container that can hold an unlimited number of values
A wrapper type that may or may not contain a value, providing a type-safe alternative to using a sentinel value or a pointer to represent 'no value'
A replacement for exceptions
A pointer that is optional to dereference
explanation: std::optional<T> represents a value that may or may not be present, avoiding the need for sentinel values (like -1) or nullable pointers to express 'no result' in a type-safe way.

questionText: What does if constexpr do in C++17?
options: It makes a normal if statement run faster at runtime
It evaluates a condition at compile time and discards the untaken branch entirely, commonly used in templates to select code per type
It replaces the switch statement
It forces both branches of an if to always execute
explanation: if constexpr (condition) evaluates the condition at compile time; the branch not taken is discarded from compilation entirely, which is especially useful for writing templates that behave differently per type without SFINAE tricks.

questionText: What is std::string_view, introduced in C++17?
options: A mutable, owning string type that replaces std::string
A lightweight, non-owning view over a contiguous sequence of characters, avoiding unnecessary string copies
A view that can only be created from string literals
A synchronization primitive for strings shared between threads
explanation: std::string_view holds a pointer and length referring to existing character data without owning or copying it, making functions that only need to read a string cheaper to call.

questionText: What is std::variant, introduced in C++17?
options: A container that stores multiple values of the same type
A type-safe tagged union that holds a value which can be one of several specified alternative types
A replacement for std::optional
A type used exclusively for error codes
explanation: std::variant<T1, T2, ...> can hold a value of exactly one of its listed alternative types at a time, giving a type-safe alternative to a raw C-style union.

questionText: What are concepts, introduced in C++20?
options: A runtime type-checking mechanism
Named compile-time predicates that constrain what types a template can accept, producing clearer errors than raw SFINAE
A new kind of comment syntax
A replacement for the auto keyword everywhere
explanation: Concepts let you express requirements on template parameters directly, e.g. template<std::integral T>, giving readable compile-time constraints and far clearer error messages than traditional SFINAE-based techniques.

questionText: What does the Ranges library add in C++20?
options: A way to define numeric ranges like Python's range() only
Composable, lazily-evaluated views and adaptors that let algorithms operate directly on ranges (containers) instead of requiring begin/end iterator pairs, and can be chained with the pipe operator
A replacement for all STL containers
A networking API for HTTP ranges
explanation: std::ranges lets algorithms work directly on a whole range instead of iterator pairs, and range adaptors (like views::filter, views::transform) can be composed lazily with the | operator.

questionText: What are coroutines, introduced in C++20?
options: A way to run multiple threads simultaneously with automatic synchronization
Functions that can suspend execution and later resume, using co_await, co_yield, or co_return, enabling asynchronous and generator-style code
A feature exclusive to lambda expressions
A new kind of exception-handling mechanism
explanation: Coroutines are functions whose execution can be suspended with co_await or co_yield and resumed later, providing language-level support for asynchronous operations and generators without manual state machines.

questionText: What is the spaceship operator (<=>), introduced in C++20?
options: An operator used only for comparing pointers
The three-way comparison operator, which can be defaulted to auto-generate all six relational operators (<, <=, >, >=, ==, !=) for a type
A bitwise operator for shifting bits
An operator that replaces the ternary conditional operator
explanation: The three-way comparison operator <=> returns an ordering result, and declaring auto operator<=>(const T&) const = default; lets the compiler generate all the relational operators automatically.

questionText: What does std::expected, introduced in C++23, provide?
options: A container that guarantees a value will never be missing
A type that holds either an expected value or an error, offering an alternative to exceptions for representing recoverable failures
A synonym for std::optional with no real difference
A type used exclusively for parsing JSON
explanation: std::expected<T, E> holds either a valid value of type T or an error of type E, letting functions report recoverable errors as part of their return type instead of throwing exceptions.

questionText: What is 'deducing this', introduced in C++23?
options: A way to remove the this pointer from member functions entirely
A feature allowing member functions to declare an explicit object parameter, letting a single function template deduce const-ness, value category, and even the derived type of the caller
A debugging tool for inspecting the this pointer at runtime
A macro that renames this to self
explanation: Deducing this lets you write an explicit object parameter (e.g. void foo(this Self&& self)) so one function template can replace multiple const/non-const or lvalue/rvalue overloads, and enables patterns like CRTP without inheritance boilerplate.

questionText: What is an array in C++?
options: A resizable collection that can grow at runtime
A fixed-size collection of elements of the same type stored contiguously in memory
A key-value data structure
A pointer to a function
explanation: A C-style array has a fixed size determined at compile time and stores its elements contiguously in memory, allowing constant-time indexed access via pointer arithmetic.

questionText: What is the key difference between a C-style string and std::string?
options: There is no difference, they are the same type
A C-style string is a null-terminated char array with manual memory management, while std::string manages its own memory and size automatically
std::string cannot hold more than 255 characters
C-style strings automatically resize themselves
explanation: A C-style string is a null-terminated array of char that requires manual buffer management, while std::string is a class that owns its buffer, tracks its length, and resizes automatically.

questionText: What is function overloading in C++?
options: Defining a function that calls itself
Defining multiple functions with the same name but different parameter lists, resolved at compile time
Replacing a base class function with a derived class version at runtime
Declaring a function without a body
explanation: Function overloading lets multiple functions share a name as long as their parameter lists differ; the compiler picks the right one at compile time based on the argument types.

questionText: What are default arguments in C++?
options: Values a compiler assigns randomly to uninitialized parameters
Values used for parameters when the caller omits the corresponding arguments
Arguments that must always be passed by reference
Arguments that can only be used in constructors
explanation: A default argument, specified in a function's declaration (e.g. void f(int x = 10)), is used automatically when the caller does not supply that argument.

questionText: What is the purpose of namespaces in C++?
options: To improve runtime performance
To group related identifiers together and avoid naming collisions between different parts of a program or libraries
To make all members of a class public
To allocate memory on the heap
explanation: Namespaces (e.g. namespace myapp { ... }) group identifiers under a named scope, preventing name clashes when different libraries or modules use the same identifier names.

questionText: Why is writing 'using namespace std;' in a header file generally discouraged?
options: It is illegal C++ and will not compile
It pulls the entire std namespace into every file that includes the header, increasing the risk of name collisions
It makes the program run more slowly
It disables the standard library entirely
explanation: Placing 'using namespace std;' in a header propagates that directive to every translation unit that includes it, greatly increasing the chance of ambiguous or unintended name clashes.

questionText: What is a key advantage of constexpr variables over preprocessor #define macros?
options: Macros are type-checked while constexpr is not
constexpr values are type-checked, scoped, and visible to the debugger, while macros are simple text substitutions with no type safety
constexpr is resolved at runtime while macros are resolved at compile time
There is no difference between them
explanation: A constexpr variable is a real, typed, scoped entity evaluated at compile time, whereas a #define macro is a blind text substitution performed by the preprocessor with no type checking or scoping.

questionText: What problem do header guards (or #pragma once) solve?
options: They speed up runtime execution
They prevent a header file's contents from being included multiple times in the same translation unit, avoiding redefinition errors
They encrypt header file contents
They allow circular includes without any restriction
explanation: Header guards (#ifndef/#define/#endif) or #pragma once ensure a header's contents are processed only once per translation unit, preventing duplicate declaration/definition errors.

questionText: What is a translation unit in C++?
options: A single line of code
The source file after preprocessing (with headers expanded), which the compiler compiles as one unit
A compiled binary executable
A single function definition
explanation: A translation unit is a source (.cpp) file together with all the headers and files it includes after preprocessing; the compiler compiles each translation unit independently before linking.

questionText: What does the One Definition Rule (ODR) state?
options: Every variable must be defined exactly once per program, but functions may be defined multiple times
An entity such as a function, class, or non-inline variable must have exactly one definition across the entire program
Only one header file may be included per source file
Only one namespace may exist per project
explanation: The One Definition Rule requires that non-inline functions, variables, classes, and templates have exactly one definition across the whole program to avoid undefined behavior and linker errors.

questionText: When is static_cast appropriate in C++?
options: For converting between unrelated pointer types with no compile-time check
For well-defined, compile-time-checked conversions such as numeric conversions or upcasting/downcasting within a known related class hierarchy
Only for casting away const
Only for reinterpreting raw memory bytes
explanation: static_cast performs conversions the compiler can verify at compile time, such as int to double, or pointer conversions within a related class hierarchy where the relationship is known.

questionText: What does dynamic_cast do in C++?
options: It converts any pointer type to any other pointer type with no checks
It performs a runtime-checked cast, typically for downcasting through a polymorphic hierarchy, returning nullptr (or throwing for references) if the cast is invalid
It removes const qualification from a pointer
It is only usable on primitive numeric types
explanation: dynamic_cast uses run-time type information (RTTI) to safely downcast within a polymorphic class hierarchy, yielding nullptr for pointers (or throwing std::bad_cast for references) on failure.

questionText: What is const_cast used for in C++?
options: Converting a pointer type to an unrelated pointer type
Adding or removing the const (or volatile) qualifier from a variable, most often to call a non-const API on data that is logically not modified
Performing arithmetic conversions between numeric types
Casting a base class pointer to a derived class pointer
explanation: const_cast adds or strips const/volatile qualifiers. Using it to modify data that was originally declared const is undefined behavior; it is mainly meant for interoperating with APIs that lack proper const-correctness.

questionText: What does reinterpret_cast do, and why is it considered dangerous?
options: It safely converts between numeric types with rounding
It reinterprets the bit pattern of one type as another unrelated type with no safety checks, which can easily lead to undefined behavior if misused
It is identical to static_cast in every way
It can only be used with smart pointers
explanation: reinterpret_cast performs low-level reinterpretation of an object's bits as a different, often unrelated type. It bypasses type safety entirely, so misuse (like aliasing violations) is undefined behavior.

questionText: What is the default member/inheritance access difference between struct and class in C++?
options: There is no difference at all between struct and class
Members and base classes are public by default in a struct, and private by default in a class
struct cannot have member functions
class cannot have public members
explanation: The only language difference between struct and class is the default access specifier: public by default for struct, private by default for class. Both can have constructors, methods, and inheritance.

questionText: Why are scoped enumerations (enum class) generally preferred over plain enums in modern C++?
options: They use less memory than plain enums
They do not implicitly convert to int and their enumerators are scoped to the enum name, preventing name clashes and accidental misuse
They can hold floating-point values
They are required for use in switch statements
explanation: enum class enumerators live in the enum's own scope (Color::Red, not just Red) and do not implicitly convert to int, avoiding the naming collisions and unsafe comparisons common with plain enums.

questionText: What is a union in C++?
options: A class that combines multiple base classes
A special class where all members share the same memory location, so only one member can hold a valid value at a time
A collection type that stores key-value pairs
A synonym for namespace
explanation: In a union, all data members occupy the same memory location, so its size is that of its largest member and only one member is valid to read at any given time.

questionText: What does the sizeof operator return in C++?
options: The number of elements in a container
The size, in bytes, that an object or type occupies in memory, evaluated at compile time
The number of bits set in a value
The memory address of a variable
explanation: sizeof is a compile-time operator that yields the size in bytes of a type or object, useful for buffer allocation and understanding memory layout (e.g. sizeof(int), sizeof(myStruct)).

questionText: What does decltype do in C++11?
options: It declares a new type alias, similar to typedef
It yields the compile-time type of an expression, which is useful in templates and for return type deduction
It converts an expression's runtime value to a string
It forces a variable to be allocated on the heap
explanation: decltype(expr) inspects an expression at compile time and yields its type, without evaluating it at runtime. It is often paired with auto for trailing return types in templates.

questionText: What does the override specifier do in C++11?
options: It makes a function run faster
It tells the compiler that a member function is intended to override a virtual function from a base class, producing a compile error if it does not actually override one
It prevents a class from being inherited
It marks a function as deprecated
explanation: override documents intent and lets the compiler verify that the function actually overrides a base class virtual function (matching signature), catching typos like mismatched parameter types at compile time.

questionText: What does the final specifier do in C++11?
options: It marks a variable as constant
It prevents a virtual function from being overridden further, or prevents a class from being inherited from, when applied to a class
It forces early evaluation of a constexpr expression
It marks a function as the program's entry point
explanation: Applied to a virtual function, final forbids derived classes from overriding it further; applied to a class definition (class Foo final), it forbids any class from inheriting from Foo.

questionText: What is uniform initialization ({}) introduced in C++11?
options: A way to initialize only arrays, not other types
A consistent brace-based syntax ({}) that can initialize aggregates, containers, and objects, and which helps prevent narrowing conversions
A macro used only in template metaprogramming
A deprecated feature removed in later standards
explanation: Uniform (brace) initialization, e.g. int x{5}; or std::vector<int> v{1,2,3};, provides one consistent syntax for initializing many kinds of objects and disallows implicit narrowing conversions.

questionText: What does static_assert do in C++11?
options: It checks a condition at runtime and logs a warning
It checks a constant expression at compile time and stops compilation with a custom message if the condition is false
It asserts that a variable is declared static
It is a synonym for the assert() macro from <cassert>
explanation: static_assert(condition, "message") is evaluated at compile time; if the condition is false, compilation fails immediately with the given message, useful for validating template parameters or type sizes.

questionText: What are delegating constructors, introduced in C++11?
options: Constructors that must be called manually after object creation
Constructors that call another constructor of the same class in their initializer list to reuse initialization logic
Constructors that are automatically generated for derived classes
A way to delegate object destruction to a helper function
explanation: A delegating constructor calls another constructor of the same class from its member-initializer list (e.g. Foo() : Foo(0) {}), avoiding duplicated initialization code across overloads.

questionText: What do the =default and =delete function specifiers do in C++11?
options: =default removes a function entirely, and =delete generates a compiler default implementation
=default explicitly requests the compiler-generated implementation of a special member function, while =delete marks a function as unusable, causing a compile error if called
They are only usable on virtual functions
They control whether a function is inlined
explanation: '= default' asks the compiler to generate the default implementation of a special member function (like a copy constructor), while '= delete' explicitly disables a function, making any use a compile-time error.

questionText: What is a trailing return type in C++11, such as auto add(int a, int b) -> int?
options: A way to return multiple values from a function
An alternative return type syntax placed after the parameter list, useful when the return type depends on the parameters (e.g. via decltype)
A type that can only be used with lambdas
A deprecated syntax removed in C++14
explanation: Trailing return type syntax (auto func(params) -> Type) places the return type after the parameters, which is necessary when the type depends on the parameters themselves, e.g. via decltype(a + b).

questionText: What changed for constexpr functions in C++11 compared to regular functions?
options: constexpr functions can never be called at runtime
A constexpr function can be evaluated at compile time when given constant expression arguments, while still being callable normally at runtime with non-constant arguments
constexpr functions cannot take any parameters
constexpr functions are automatically inlined into machine code as a macro
explanation: A C++11 constexpr function can produce a compile-time constant when its arguments are constant expressions, but it remains an ordinary callable function usable at runtime with non-constant arguments too.

questionText: What is the [[noreturn]] attribute, introduced in C++11, used for?
options: To mark a function that always returns a value
To indicate to the compiler that a function never returns to its caller (e.g. it always throws or calls std::exit), enabling better diagnostics and optimizations
To prevent a function from being called recursively
To disable return value optimization
explanation: [[noreturn]] tells the compiler a function will never return control to its caller (it always throws, aborts, or loops forever), which can suppress false 'missing return' warnings and enable optimizations.

questionText: What are init-captures (generalized lambda captures), introduced in C++14?
options: A way to capture variables by reference only
A lambda capture syntax that allows declaring and initializing a new variable in the capture list, e.g. [x = std::move(y)]
A restriction that forbids capturing local variables
A feature exclusive to global lambdas
explanation: C++14 init-captures let a lambda's capture list introduce a new variable with its own initializer, e.g. [value = computeSomething()], which is also how you move a variable into a lambda's closure.

questionText: What are binary literals and digit separators, both introduced in C++14?
options: Features for formatting output streams
Binary literals let you write integers in base 2 with a 0b prefix (0b1010), and digit separators use a single quote to group digits for readability (1'000'000)
A way to convert strings to binary data
A deprecated numeric formatting style
explanation: C++14 added 0b/0B binary integer literals (e.g. 0b1010 == 10) and the digit separator ' to make large numeric literals easier to read, e.g. 1'000'000.

questionText: What is the [[deprecated]] attribute, introduced in C++14?
options: It removes a function from the binary entirely
It marks a declaration as discouraged for use, causing the compiler to emit a warning at each use site
It forces a function to be inlined
It disables all warnings for that function
explanation: [[deprecated]] (optionally with a message, [[deprecated("use bar() instead")]]) marks an entity as discouraged, so the compiler warns callers without breaking existing builds.

questionText: What did C++14 add regarding return type deduction for ordinary functions?
options: Nothing changed; auto return types were always allowed for regular functions
C++14 allows a regular function to use plain auto as its return type, letting the compiler deduce it from the return statement(s), extending what C++11 only allowed for lambdas
It removed the ability to specify explicit return types
It only applies to constructors
explanation: C++11 allowed auto return type deduction only for lambdas (with a single return statement). C++14 extended this to ordinary functions and lambdas with multiple returns, as long as all returns agree on type.

questionText: What is std::any, introduced in C++17?
options: A container that can only hold integers
A type-safe container that can hold a value of virtually any single type, queried and retrieved via std::any_cast
A synonym for void*
A container for holding multiple unrelated values simultaneously like a tuple
explanation: std::any is a type-safe container for a single value of any copyable type, decided at runtime. Its contained value is retrieved with std::any_cast<T>, which throws std::bad_any_cast on a type mismatch.

questionText: What is Class Template Argument Deduction (CTAD), introduced in C++17?
options: A way to forbid templates from being instantiated with certain types
A feature that lets the compiler deduce a class template's type parameters from constructor arguments, so you can write std::pair p(1, 2.0); instead of specifying template arguments explicitly
A runtime mechanism for checking template types
A feature exclusive to function templates
explanation: CTAD lets you write std::vector v{1, 2, 3}; or std::pair p(1, 2.0); and have the compiler deduce the template arguments from the constructor call, without needing to spell them out explicitly.

questionText: What are fold expressions, introduced in C++17?
options: A way to fold (compress) a data structure to save memory
A concise syntax for applying a binary operator over all elements of a parameter pack in a variadic template, e.g. (args + ...)
A technique for folding recursive function calls into loops automatically
A method for merging two classes into one at compile time
explanation: Fold expressions let you write (args + ...) or (... + args) to apply a binary operator across all elements of a parameter pack in a variadic template, avoiding manual recursive unpacking.

questionText: What are inline variables, introduced in C++17?
options: Variables that are always stored in CPU registers
Variables that can be defined in a header file and included in multiple translation units without violating the One Definition Rule
Variables that cannot be modified after initialization
A synonym for constexpr variables
explanation: An inline variable (inline int counter = 0;) may be defined identically in multiple translation units (e.g. via a header) without ODR violations, similar to how inline functions have long worked.

questionText: What does an if or switch statement with an init-statement, introduced in C++17, look like and do?
options: if (int x; x > 0) is invalid syntax in C++17
It lets you declare and initialize a variable scoped to the if/switch statement itself, e.g. if (auto it = m.find(k); it != m.end()) { ... }, keeping the variable out of the enclosing scope
It replaces the need for braces around if bodies
It only works with switch statements, not if statements
explanation: C++17 allows an init-statement inside if/switch, e.g. if (auto it = m.find(key); it != m.end()) {...}, scoping the declared variable to the statement and its branches instead of leaking into the surrounding scope.

questionText: What does the [[nodiscard]] attribute, introduced in C++17, do?
options: It forces a function's return value to be discarded automatically
It causes the compiler to warn if a function's return value is ignored by the caller, helping catch bugs like ignoring an error code
It prevents a function from being called more than once
It marks a variable as unused
explanation: [[nodiscard]] on a function (or type) makes the compiler emit a warning if the caller discards its return value, which is useful for catching ignored error codes or accidentally-unused results.

questionText: What does the [[maybe_unused]] attribute, introduced in C++17, do?
options: It marks a variable for garbage collection
It suppresses compiler warnings about an entity (variable, parameter, etc.) that is intentionally left unused
It forces a variable to always be used at least once
It deletes a variable at compile time
explanation: [[maybe_unused]] tells the compiler not to warn about an unused entity, useful for parameters that are only used conditionally (e.g. only in debug builds) but must still appear in the signature.

questionText: What is std::byte, introduced in C++17?
options: A synonym for int used to save memory
A distinct type representing raw memory as a single byte, supporting only bitwise operations rather than arithmetic or implicit conversion to/from integers or characters
A container that stores exactly 8 bits as a bitset
A deprecated alias for unsigned char
explanation: std::byte is an enum class-based type meant to represent raw memory. It supports bitwise operators but, unlike char or unsigned char, does not implicitly convert to/from integer types, improving type safety.

questionText: What are C++20 modules intended to replace or improve upon?
options: The dynamic linker at runtime
The traditional #include header mechanism, by allowing code to be organized into modules that are compiled once and imported, improving build times and reducing macro/name leakage
The C++ template system entirely
The standard library's container classes
explanation: Modules (import std; or user-defined modules) let code be compiled once and imported elsewhere without textual header inclusion, avoiding repeated parsing, macro leakage, and many ODR pitfalls of headers.

questionText: What does consteval, introduced in C++20, mean when applied to a function?
options: The function can optionally run at compile time or runtime, like constexpr
The function must be evaluated entirely at compile time; calling it in a context that requires a runtime value is a compile error
The function can only be called from constexpr contexts, but always executes at runtime
It marks a function as thread-safe
explanation: Unlike constexpr (which may or may not run at compile time), a consteval function is an 'immediate function' that must produce a compile-time constant every time it is called, or the program fails to compile.

questionText: What does constinit, introduced in C++20, guarantee?
options: That a variable is initialized lazily on first use

That a variable with static storage duration is initialized with a constant expression at compile time, preventing the 'static initialization order fiasco', while still allowing the variable to be mutable afterward
That a variable can never be modified after initialization
That a variable is thread-local
explanation: constinit ensures a variable is initialized at compile time (avoiding dynamic/static initialization order issues across translation units) but, unlike constexpr, does not make the variable itself immutable afterward.

questionText: What is std::span, introduced in C++20?
options: An owning container similar to std::vector
A lightweight, non-owning view over a contiguous sequence of elements (such as an array or part of a vector), providing bounds information without copying data
A fixed-size replacement for std::array
A type used exclusively for string manipulation
explanation: std::span<T> is a non-owning 'view' referring to a contiguous block of elements (e.g. a C array, std::vector, or std::array) along with its size, without copying or owning the underlying data.

questionText: What are designated initializers, introduced in C++20?
options: A way to initialize only the first member of an aggregate
A syntax that lets you initialize specific named members of an aggregate (struct) by name, e.g. Point p{.x = 1, .y = 2}
A feature for initializing pointers to null automatically
A macro-based initialization technique
explanation: Designated initializers allow aggregate initialization to name the members being set, e.g. Point p{.x = 1, .y = 2}, improving clarity about which member receives which value.

questionText: What is char8_t, introduced in C++20?
options: A synonym for char that behaves identically in every context
A distinct type for representing UTF-8 code units, used for u8 string literals, distinguishing UTF-8 text from plain char or unsigned char data
An 8-bit floating point type
A type used only for file paths
explanation: char8_t is a new distinct type (not just an alias for char) used for UTF-8 code units in u8"..." literals, giving UTF-8 text a distinct type from ordinary char or unsigned char data.

questionText: What does std::format, introduced in C++20, provide?
options: A way to format hard disks from within a C++ program
A type-safe, Python-style string formatting facility (e.g. std::format("{} is {}", name, age)) as a safer alternative to printf-style formatting
A replacement for the entire iostream library
A tool for formatting source code automatically
explanation: std::format offers positional, type-safe string formatting similar to Python's str.format, e.g. std::format("{} is {} years old", name, age), catching type mismatches at compile time where possible.

questionText: What is std::print, introduced in C++23?
options: A macro identical to the C printf function
A convenient function that combines std::format-style formatting with direct output to a stream (defaulting to stdout), without needing std::cout or a separate format call
A debugging tool that only works in debug builds
A function that can only print to files, not to the console
explanation: std::print("{} plus {} is {}\n", a, b, a + b) combines std::format's safe formatting with direct output, letting you print formatted text in one call without manually building a string or chaining << operators.

questionText: What does 'if consteval', introduced in C++23, let you do?
options: Check at runtime whether a value is a compile-time constant
Branch a function's logic based on whether it is currently being evaluated in a compile-time (constant evaluation) context or at runtime, useful inside constexpr functions
Replace all if statements in constexpr functions
Force a function to always evaluate at compile time
explanation: 'if consteval { ... } else { ... }' lets a constexpr function choose different code paths depending on whether it is currently executing during compile-time evaluation or at runtime.

questionText: What does the C++23 multidimensional subscript operator allow you to write?
options: Nothing new; operator[] never accepted more than one argument
operator[] can now take multiple arguments, e.g. matrix[row, col], instead of requiring a workaround like matrix[row][col] or matrix(row, col)
It removes support for operator[] entirely in favor of .at()
It only applies to std::vector, not to user-defined types
explanation: Before C++23, operator[] accepted exactly one argument, so multi-dimensional access needed operator() or chained [][]. C++23 allows operator[] to take multiple arguments, e.g. matrix[row, col].

questionText: What does the C++23 std::stacktrace library provide?
options: A way to manually manage the call stack's memory
A portable, standard way to capture and print the current call stack for diagnostics, without relying on platform-specific debugging APIs
A replacement for exception handling entirely
A tool exclusively for measuring function execution time
explanation: std::stacktrace lets code capture the current call stack (e.g. std::stacktrace::current()) and print it, giving portable diagnostic output similar to what debuggers show, without OS-specific APIs.

questionText: What is an abbreviated function template, a C++20 feature that lets you write void f(auto x) instead of a template<typename T> declaration?
options: A syntax error in all versions of C++
A shorthand where using auto as a function parameter type implicitly makes the function a template, deducing the parameter's type from the call site just like a normal template parameter
A way to declare a function without specifying any parameter types at all
A feature that only works for lambda parameters, not regular functions
explanation: C++20 allows 'auto' as a function parameter type, e.g. void f(auto x), which implicitly turns f into a function template equivalent to template<typename T> void f(T x), deducing T per call.

questionText: How does std::vector typically grow its internal storage as elements are added, and what does capacity() vs size() mean?
options: It reallocates on every single push_back call, so capacity always equals size
It grows its capacity in larger chunks (often doubling) as needed, so size() is the number of elements while capacity() is how many elements can be held before the next reallocation
It never reallocates once created; the initial capacity is fixed forever
capacity() and size() always return the same value
explanation: std::vector amortizes growth by allocating extra capacity (commonly doubling) so push_back is amortized O(1). size() is the current element count; capacity() is how many elements fit before a reallocation is needed.

questionText: How does std::array (C++11) differ from a plain C-style array?
options: std::array can resize itself at runtime, unlike a C-style array
std::array wraps a fixed-size C-style array in a class that knows its own size, supports iterators, bounds-checked access via at(), and works well with STL algorithms
std::array is always slower than a C-style array
std::array can only store pointers
explanation: std::array<T, N> is a thin, zero-overhead wrapper around a fixed-size array that adds a size() method, iterators, bounds-checked at() access, and compatibility with STL algorithms, all with compile-time fixed size.

questionText: What is the underlying structure and main trade-off of std::list?
options: It is a contiguous array offering O(1) random access but slow insertion
It is a doubly linked list offering O(1) insertion/removal anywhere given an iterator, but only sequential (not random) access to elements
It is a hash table with no ordering guarantees
It is identical in performance characteristics to std::vector
explanation: std::list is a doubly linked list: inserting or erasing at any position is O(1) given an iterator to that position, but there is no random access, so reaching the nth element takes O(n).

questionText: What is std::forward_list, introduced in C++11?
options: A doubly linked list identical to std::list
A singly linked list, more memory-efficient than std::list since each node stores only one 'next' pointer, but without operations like size() or backward traversal
A container that only stores forward iterators
A thread-safe version of std::list
explanation: std::forward_list is a singly linked list, using less memory per node than std::list (no 'previous' pointer) at the cost of not supporting backward traversal or an O(1) size() member.

questionText: What is std::deque, and how does it differ from std::vector?
options: It is identical to std::vector in every respect
A double-ended queue that supports efficient O(1) insertion/removal at both the front and back, unlike std::vector which is only efficient at the back
It only supports insertion at the front, never at the back
It cannot be accessed with the [] operator
explanation: std::deque provides random access like std::vector, but also supports efficient O(1) push_front/pop_front, unlike std::vector where inserting at the front is O(n) since all elements must shift.

questionText: What guarantees does std::set provide about its elements?
options: Elements are unordered and duplicates are allowed
Elements are unique and automatically kept in sorted order (by operator< or a custom comparator), typically implemented as a balanced binary search tree with O(log n) operations
Elements are stored in insertion order with no sorting
It allows duplicate elements but keeps them sorted
explanation: std::set stores unique elements in sorted order, usually backed by a red-black tree, giving O(log n) insertion, lookup, and removal, with in-order iteration producing sorted output.

questionText: How does std::multiset differ from std::set?
options: std::multiset does not keep elements sorted
std::multiset allows multiple elements that compare equal (duplicates), while std::set requires all elements to be unique
std::multiset can only store numeric types
std::multiset is unordered, like std::unordered_set
explanation: std::multiset has the same sorted, tree-based structure as std::set, but permits multiple elements with equivalent keys, whereas std::set enforces uniqueness.

questionText: How does std::map determine the order in which keys are stored and iterated?
options: By insertion order only
Keys are kept sorted according to operator< by default, or a custom comparator supplied as a template argument, since std::map is typically backed by a balanced binary search tree
By the hash value of each key
std::map does not guarantee any particular order
explanation: std::map keeps its key-value pairs sorted by key, using operator< by default (or a custom comparator), backed by a balanced tree, so in-order traversal visits keys in ascending order.

questionText: How does std::multimap differ from std::map?
options: std::multimap does not associate keys with values
std::multimap allows multiple entries with the same key, while std::map requires each key to be unique
std::multimap is hash-based while std::map is tree-based
std::multimap cannot be iterated in sorted order
explanation: std::multimap has the same sorted, tree-based design as std::map, but allows several entries to share the same key, unlike std::map where each key maps to exactly one value.

questionText: What must be true of a key type used in std::unordered_map, introduced in C++11?
options: The key type must support operator< for ordering
The key type must be hashable (via std::hash or a custom hash functor) and support equality comparison, since the container uses a hash table rather than sorted order
The key type must be a built-in numeric type
The key type must be copyable but not movable
explanation: std::unordered_map is backed by a hash table, so keys need a valid hash (via std::hash<Key> or a custom specialization) and an equality comparison, giving average O(1) lookup/insert but no ordering.

questionText: What is std::unordered_set, introduced in C++11?
options: A sorted collection of unique keys, like std::set but hash-based instead of tree-based
A hash-table-based container storing unique elements with no defined iteration order, offering average O(1) insertion, lookup, and removal
A container that allows duplicate elements and preserves insertion order
A synonym for std::unordered_map with no values
explanation: std::unordered_set stores unique elements in a hash table, trading the sorted order and O(log n) operations of std::set for average O(1) operations, with an unspecified iteration order.

questionText: What kind of container is std::stack, and what is its underlying default container?
options: It is a first-in-first-out (FIFO) adapter always backed by std::list
It is a container adapter providing last-in-first-out (LIFO) access (push/pop/top), by default implemented on top of std::deque
It is a raw memory buffer with no push/pop operations
It is always backed by std::vector and cannot use any other container
explanation: std::stack is a container adapter exposing only LIFO operations (push, pop, top). It wraps an underlying sequence container, std::deque by default, though std::vector or std::list can also be used.

questionText: What kind of container is std::queue, and what access pattern does it provide?
options: A LIFO (last-in-first-out) adapter identical to std::stack
A container adapter providing first-in-first-out (FIFO) access, with elements pushed at the back and popped from the front
A container that allows random access to any element by index
A container that automatically sorts its elements
explanation: std::queue is a FIFO container adapter: elements are added with push() at the back and removed with pop() from the front, modeling a waiting line, typically backed by std::deque.

questionText: What does std::priority_queue provide, and what is its default underlying container?
options: FIFO ordering backed by std::list
A container adapter that always gives access to the largest element first (a max-heap by default), typically implemented using std::vector with heap algorithms
Strict insertion-order access with no reordering
Sorted iteration over all elements, like std::set
explanation: std::priority_queue keeps elements in a heap structure (max-heap by default) so top() always returns the largest element per the comparator; it is typically implemented atop std::vector using make_heap/push_heap/pop_heap.

questionText: What does std::tie, used with std::tuple, let you do?
options: Merge two tuples into a single larger tuple
Unpack a tuple's (or pair's) elements into existing variables by reference, e.g. std::tie(a, b) = someTuple;
Convert a tuple into a std::vector
Compare two tuples for equality
explanation: std::tie(a, b, c) creates a tuple of references to the given variables, so assigning a tuple to it (std::tie(a, b) = getPair();) unpacks the tuple's values into those existing variables.

questionText: How do you access an individual element of a std::tuple by position?
options: Using the [] operator, like tuple[0]
Using std::get<N>(myTuple), where N is a compile-time index (or the element's type, if unique in the tuple)
Using the .at(N) member function
Tuple elements cannot be accessed individually, only as a whole
explanation: std::tuple elements are accessed with the free function std::get<N>(t), where N is a compile-time constant index, since tuple elements can have different types and operator[] cannot express that.

questionText: What is the difference between an iterator and a const_iterator in the STL?
options: There is no difference; they are interchangeable in all containers
A const_iterator allows read access to elements but prevents modifying them through the iterator, while a plain iterator allows both reading and writing
const_iterator can only be used with std::vector
A const_iterator is always slower than a regular iterator
explanation: Both traverse a container the same way, but dereferencing a const_iterator yields a reference-to-const, preventing modification of the underlying element, while a plain iterator allows mutation.

questionText: What are the requirements and typical complexity of std::sort from <algorithm>?
options: It works on any container and runs in O(n) time
It requires random-access iterators (like those of std::vector or std::array) and has an average/worst-case complexity of O(n log n)
It only works on already-partially-sorted ranges
It requires the elements to be unique
explanation: std::sort needs random-access iterators, so it works directly on std::vector, std::array, or deque (but not std::list, which has its own sort() member), and guarantees O(n log n) complexity.

questionText: What does std::find, from <algorithm>, return when searching a range for a value?
options: The index of the value as an integer
An iterator to the first matching element, or the end iterator of the range if no match is found
A boolean indicating whether the value exists
A copy of the entire range with the value removed
explanation: std::find(first, last, value) performs a linear O(n) scan and returns an iterator to the first element equal to value, or the 'last' iterator if the value is not present in the range.

questionText: What does std::transform, from <algorithm>, do?
options: It sorts a range in place
It applies a given function to each element of an input range and writes the results to a destination range (which can be the same range)
It removes all elements matching a predicate
It converts a container to a different container type automatically
explanation: std::transform(first, last, dest, func) applies func to each element in [first, last) and stores each result into the destination range starting at dest, which may overlap with the source.

questionText: What does std::accumulate, from <numeric>, do?
options: It counts the number of elements in a range
It folds a range into a single value by repeatedly applying an operation (addition by default, or a custom binary function) starting from an initial value
It sorts elements and removes duplicates
It reserves memory for a container in advance
explanation: std::accumulate(first, last, init) combines all elements in the range with init using operator+ by default (or a custom binary function passed as a fourth argument), commonly used to sum a range.

questionText: What is the key difference between push_back and emplace_back on containers like std::vector, introduced in C++11?
options: They are completely identical with no difference at all

emplace_back constructs the new element in place using the given arguments (forwarding them to the element's constructor), potentially avoiding a temporary object and extra copy/move that push_back may require
push_back is faster than emplace_back in every case
emplace_back can only be used with primitive types like int
explanation: emplace_back forwards its arguments directly to the element type's constructor, constructing the object in place inside the container's storage, whereas push_back typically takes an already-constructed object to copy or move in.

questionText: What can happen to existing iterators and references when std::vector reallocates due to push_back exceeding capacity?
options: Nothing; iterators and references always remain valid
All existing iterators, pointers, and references to elements become invalidated because the elements are moved or copied to a new memory block
Only the end() iterator becomes invalid
Only references become invalid, but iterators stay valid
explanation: When a vector's size exceeds its capacity, it allocates a new, larger buffer and moves/copies all elements there, invalidating every iterator, pointer, and reference into the old buffer.

questionText: What does std::unique, from <algorithm>, actually do to a range?
options: It removes all duplicate values anywhere in the range, regardless of order
It removes consecutive duplicate elements, moving unique elements to the front and returning a new logical end; it must be run on an already-sorted range to remove all duplicates
It sorts the range and removes the smallest half of the elements
It throws an exception if any duplicate elements are found
explanation: std::unique only removes adjacent (consecutive) duplicates, returning an iterator marking the new logical end; to eliminate all duplicates regardless of position, the range must be sorted first.

questionText: What is std::bitset, and how does it differ from std::vector<bool>?
options: It is a dynamically resizable array of booleans
It represents a fixed-size (compile-time-known) sequence of bits with efficient bitwise operations (AND, OR, XOR, shifts) and no dynamic resizing
It stores each bit as a full byte, wasting memory
It can only be used to store true/false flags, with no bitwise operators
explanation: std::bitset<N> has a fixed size N known at compile time and provides efficient bitwise operators and functions like count(), set(), flip(), unlike std::vector<bool> which is dynamically sized.

questionText: What is a function template in C++?
options: A function that can only be called once
A blueprint for generating functions that work with different types, where the compiler generates a concrete function for each type it is instantiated with
A function pointer stored in a struct
A macro that expands into multiple functions
explanation: A function template, e.g. template<typename T> T max(T a, T b), lets the compiler generate a type-specific version of the function for each distinct type it is called with, avoiding repetitive overloads.

questionText: What is a class template in C++?
options: A class that can never be instantiated
A blueprint for generating classes parameterized by one or more types, such as std::vector<T>, where the compiler generates a concrete class for each type used
An abstract base class with only pure virtual functions
A class restricted to holding exactly one member variable
explanation: A class template (e.g. template<typename T> class Box {...}) defines a family of classes parameterized by type; std::vector, std::map, and similar containers are all class templates.

questionText: What is full template specialization?
options: Making a template work with any type by adding more parameters
Providing a completely custom implementation of a template for one specific set of template arguments, overriding the generic template for that exact case
Deleting a template so it can no longer be instantiated
A way to make templates run faster automatically for all types
explanation: Full specialization (template<> class Box<int> {...}) provides a distinct implementation used only when the template is instantiated with that exact set of arguments, overriding the generic definition.

questionText: What is partial template specialization?
options: Specializing a template for exactly one specific type only
Providing a specialized implementation of a class template that still has some template parameters left generic, e.g. specializing Box<T*> for all pointer types T
A feature available only for function templates, not class templates
Removing part of a template's member functions
explanation: Partial specialization customizes a class template for a subset of possible arguments while keeping some parameters generic, e.g. template<typename T> class Box<T*> {...} specializes for any pointer type.

questionText: What does SFINAE ('Substitution Failure Is Not An Error') mean in template metaprogramming?
options: Any substitution failure in a template always causes a hard compile error

When substituting template arguments produces an invalid type or expression for a candidate, that candidate is simply removed from overload resolution instead of causing a compile error, as long as other viable candidates exist
Templates cannot fail to compile under any circumstances
It refers to a runtime error-handling mechanism
explanation: SFINAE means that if substituting specific template arguments into a candidate produces an invalid construct, that candidate is silently dropped from overload resolution rather than causing a hard error, enabling techniques like enable_if.

questionText: What do type traits, such as std::is_integral or std::is_pointer from <type_traits>, provide?
options: Runtime functions for converting between types
Compile-time boolean or type information about a given type, usable in template metaprogramming to enable or disable code paths based on type properties
A way to change a variable's type after it has been declared
Tools for serializing objects to disk
explanation: Type traits like std::is_integral<T>::value are compile-time constants describing properties of a type, commonly used with if constexpr or SFINAE to select different template code paths based on the type.

questionText: Why is std::make_shared generally preferred over std::shared_ptr<T>(new T(...))?
