options: make_shared disables reference counting for better performance
make_shared allocates the control block and the managed object together in a single memory allocation, improving performance and exception safety compared to two separate allocations
make_shared can only be used with primitive types
There is no difference between the two approaches
explanation: std::shared_ptr<T>(new T()) performs two allocations (the object and a separate control block), while std::make_shared<T>() combines them into a single allocation, which is faster and safer against certain exception scenarios.

questionText: What does inheriting from std::enable_shared_from_this allow a class to do?
options: Automatically delete itself when no longer needed
Safely obtain a std::shared_ptr to 'this' from within a member function, sharing ownership with any existing shared_ptr instances that manage the object
Prevent the object from ever being managed by a shared_ptr
Convert itself into a weak_ptr automatically
explanation: A class inheriting from std::enable_shared_from_this<T> can call shared_from_this() inside a member function to get a valid shared_ptr to itself that correctly shares the existing control block, rather than creating a separate, conflicting one.

questionText: What problem does std::weak_ptr, introduced in C++11, solve?
options: It makes shared_ptr objects thread-safe
It allows observing an object managed by shared_ptr without contributing to its reference count, breaking reference cycles that would otherwise prevent shared_ptrs from ever reaching zero references
It replaces shared_ptr entirely for all use cases
It converts raw pointers into shared_ptr automatically
explanation: std::weak_ptr holds a non-owning reference to an object managed by shared_ptr, letting code check if the object still exists (via lock()) without keeping it alive, which breaks reference cycles between shared_ptrs.

questionText: What is copy elision / Named Return Value Optimization (NRVO)?
options: A runtime technique for compressing copied objects

A compiler optimization that avoids constructing and then copying/moving a temporary object, instead constructing it directly at its final destination, such as directly in the caller's storage when returning by value
A rule that forbids returning objects by value
A feature that only applies to primitive types like int
explanation: Copy elision (including NRVO) lets the compiler construct a returned object directly in the caller's destination storage, skipping the copy or move construction that would otherwise occur, improving performance.

questionText: What does marking a single-argument constructor explicit prevent?
options: It prevents the constructor from ever being called
It prevents the constructor from being used for implicit conversions, e.g. it stops code like MyClass obj = 5; from silently converting 5 into a MyClass
It forces the constructor to always throw an exception
It makes the class unable to be copied
explanation: Without explicit, a single-argument (or otherwise convertible) constructor allows implicit conversions, e.g. passing an int where a MyClass is expected. Marking it explicit requires callers to construct the object directly.

questionText: What is Argument-Dependent Lookup (ADL), also known as Koenig lookup?
options: A rule that forbids overloaded functions from being called with arguments of different types

A lookup rule where, for a function call, the compiler also searches namespaces associated with the argument types, not just the immediately visible scope, which is why calling swap(a, b) can find a namespace-specific swap overload
A runtime mechanism for resolving virtual function calls
A feature exclusive to template metaprogramming
explanation: ADL extends unqualified name lookup for function calls to also search the namespaces of the argument types, which is why std::swap can be found and overridden by a type-specific swap in that type's own namespace.

questionText: What is the 'Rule of Zero' in modern C++ class design?
options: Every class must explicitly define all five special member functions

A class should avoid manually managing raw resources at all, instead composing it from members like smart pointers and standard containers that already manage their own resources, so no special member functions need to be written by hand
Classes should never have any member variables
Constructors should never take any parameters
explanation: The Rule of Zero says that by delegating resource management to members like std::unique_ptr, std::vector, or std::string, a class needs no custom destructor, copy, or move operations at all, since the compiler-generated defaults already do the right thing.

questionText: What is operator overloading, and what is one important limitation on it in C++?
options: It lets you define custom behavior for operators like + or == on user-defined types, but you cannot invent new operator symbols or change an operator's arity/precedence
It allows creating entirely new operators with custom symbols
It lets you change how built-in types like int behave with existing operators
It only works for the assignment operator
explanation: Operator overloading lets a class define what operators like +, ==, or << mean for its objects, but C++ does not allow inventing new operator tokens or changing an existing operator's number of operands or precedence.

questionText: How does a virtual function enable dynamic (runtime) polymorphism in C++?
options: The compiler always calls the base class version, regardless of the actual object type
A call through a base class pointer or reference is resolved at runtime via a vtable lookup, invoking the most-derived override for the object's actual dynamic type
Virtual functions are resolved entirely at compile time based on the static type
Virtual functions can only be called on stack-allocated objects
explanation: When a function is declared virtual, calling it through a base class pointer/reference is dispatched at runtime using a vtable, so the override defined in the object's actual (most-derived) type is executed.

questionText: What is a pure virtual function, and what does it make a class?
options: A virtual function with no implementation at all, declared with '= 0', which makes the class abstract and unable to be instantiated directly
A function that can only be called once per object
A virtual function that is automatically inlined
A function that must be implemented identically in every derived class
explanation: A pure virtual function (virtual void f() = 0;) has no implementation in that class, making the class abstract; it cannot be instantiated until a derived class provides an override for every pure virtual function.

questionText: Why should a base class's destructor be declared virtual if the class is meant to be used polymorphically?
options: It is never necessary; all destructors behave the same regardless

Without a virtual destructor, deleting a derived object through a base class pointer only calls the base class destructor, skipping the derived class's cleanup and causing undefined behavior or resource leaks
A virtual destructor makes object construction faster
It is only needed for classes with no member variables
explanation: If delete is called on a base class pointer to a derived object and the destructor is not virtual, only the base class's destructor runs, leaving the derived part's resources uncleaned - a common source of bugs and leaks.

questionText: What is the 'diamond problem' in multiple inheritance?
options: A performance issue that only affects template classes
When a class inherits from two classes that both inherit from a common base, the derived class ends up with two separate copies of that common base's members unless virtual inheritance is used
A syntax error that prevents multiple inheritance from compiling
An issue that only occurs with virtual functions, never with data members
explanation: If classes B and C both inherit from A, and class D inherits from both B and C, D ends up with two separate A subobjects (ambiguous access) unless A is inherited virtually by B and C, giving D a single shared A subobject.

questionText: How does virtual inheritance solve the diamond problem?
options: It removes the shared base class entirely from the hierarchy
It ensures that only a single shared instance of the common base class is included in the most-derived object, no matter how many paths lead to it in the inheritance hierarchy
It makes all inherited functions virtual automatically
It forbids classes from inheriting from more than one base class
explanation: When intermediate classes inherit from a common base using 'virtual' (e.g. class B : public virtual A), the most-derived class contains only one shared subobject of A, eliminating the ambiguity of the diamond problem.

questionText: What does the friend keyword allow in C++?
options: It lets any class access the private members of any other class automatically
It grants a specific external function or class explicit access to the private and protected members of the class that declares it as a friend
It makes a class's members public permanently
It creates a copy of a class with all members made public
explanation: Declaring 'friend class X;' or 'friend void f();' inside a class grants that specific class or function access to the declaring class's private and protected members, as an explicit, targeted exception to encapsulation.

questionText: How does exception handling with try/catch/throw work in C++?
options: throw silently logs an error and continues execution normally
throw raises an exception object which propagates up the call stack, unwinding it (destroying local objects along the way) until a matching catch block handles it
Exceptions can only be caught in the same function where they are thrown
catch blocks must always be written before the corresponding try block
explanation: When 'throw expr;' executes, the runtime unwinds the call stack, calling destructors of local objects along the way, until it finds a catch block whose parameter type matches the thrown exception's type.

questionText: What is the difference between the basic and strong exception safety guarantees?
options: They are the same thing with different names

The basic guarantee ensures no resources are leaked and invariants hold after an exception, while the strong guarantee additionally ensures the operation either fully succeeds or leaves the object completely unchanged (as if it never happened)
The strong guarantee only applies to constructors
The basic guarantee means no exceptions can ever be thrown
explanation: Basic guarantee: after an exception, no leaks occur and the object remains in a valid (but possibly modified) state. Strong guarantee: the operation is transactional - it either completes fully or has no visible effect at all.

questionText: What does the noexcept specifier, introduced in C++11, communicate about a function?
options: That the function's body contains no exception-related code at all, checked by the compiler
That the function promises not to throw any exceptions; if it does throw anyway, std::terminate is called instead of normal stack unwinding
That the function can only be called inside a try block
That the function is automatically optimized to run faster with no other effect
explanation: noexcept declares that a function will not throw. If a noexcept function does throw, std::terminate is invoked immediately rather than propagating the exception, and it also enables certain optimizations (e.g. in std::vector's move operations).

questionText: How do you define a custom exception type that integrates well with standard exception handling?
options: By defining any unrelated class and throwing an instance of it
By deriving from std::exception (or one of its standard subclasses like std::runtime_error) and overriding the what() member function to describe the error
Custom exception types are not supported in C++; only built-in types can be thrown
By making the exception type a template with no base class
explanation: Deriving from std::exception (or std::runtime_error/std::logic_error) and overriding what() lets custom exceptions be caught generically via catch (const std::exception&) while still providing a descriptive message.

questionText: What is placement new used for in C++?
options: It allocates a new block of heap memory, just like a normal new expression
It constructs an object at a specific, already-allocated memory address, without allocating new memory itself, which is useful for custom allocators and memory pools
It is a synonym for malloc that also zero-initializes memory
It replaces the need for destructors entirely
explanation: Placement new, 'new (ptr) T(args)', constructs a T object at the pre-allocated address 'ptr' rather than allocating new storage, commonly used in custom allocators, memory pools, and low-level containers.

questionText: What is alignas, introduced in C++11, used for?
options: To reduce the memory footprint of a type as much as possible
To specify a stricter (larger) memory alignment requirement for a variable or type than its natural default, which can matter for SIMD instructions or hardware requirements
To disable memory alignment entirely for a type
To align text output printed to the console
explanation: alignas(N) lets you request that a type or object be aligned to an N-byte boundary, which can be required for SIMD data types, cache-line alignment, or interfacing with hardware/DMA buffers that have alignment requirements.

questionText: What is a bit-field in a C++ struct or class, such as 'unsigned int flag : 1;'?
options: A member that must always occupy a full byte regardless of its declared width
A member declared to occupy a specific number of bits rather than a whole byte or word, useful for tightly packing flags or small values, though layout details are implementation-defined
A special kind of virtual function
A synonym for std::bitset
explanation: A bit-field like 'unsigned int flag : 1;' tells the compiler to pack that member into just 1 bit (or however many are specified) rather than a full storage unit, useful for compact flag storage, though exact packing/order is implementation-defined.

questionText: What is the Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (CRTP)?
options: A pattern where a class inherits from itself directly

A pattern where a class Derived inherits from a base class template instantiated with Derived itself, e.g. class Derived : public Base<Derived>, enabling static (compile-time) polymorphism without virtual functions
A naming convention for recursive functions
A deprecated technique replaced entirely by concepts in C++20
explanation: In CRTP, 'class Derived : public Base<Derived>' lets Base access Derived's members via static_cast<Derived*>(this), achieving compile-time ('static') polymorphism with no virtual function call overhead.

questionText: What is the PImpl (Pointer to Implementation) idiom used for?
options: To make a class's private members public
To hide a class's implementation details behind a pointer to a forward-declared implementation class, reducing header dependencies and improving compile-time isolation and binary compatibility
To automatically implement a class's virtual functions
To convert a class into a template
explanation: PImpl moves a class's private data/implementation into a separate class accessed via a pointer, with only a forward declaration in the header, which hides implementation details, speeds up rebuilds, and can preserve ABI stability.

questionText: What do std::function and std::bind, introduced in C++11, provide?
options: std::function is a container for storing multiple functions of different signatures together

std::function is a general-purpose, type-erased wrapper that can hold any callable (function pointer, lambda, functor) matching a given signature, and std::bind creates a new callable by binding some arguments of an existing callable
They are both deprecated in favor of raw function pointers
std::bind is used only for binding network sockets
explanation: std::function<Ret(Args...)> can store any callable matching that signature (lambda, function pointer, functor), while std::bind(f, arg1, std::placeholders::_1) produces a new callable with some arguments pre-bound.

questionText: What does std::thread, introduced in C++11, represent?
options: A lightweight coroutine that runs cooperatively on the same OS thread
An object representing a single thread of execution, which begins running a given callable as soon as the std::thread object is constructed
A pool of reusable worker threads managed automatically
A synonym for std::async
explanation: A std::thread object launches a new thread of execution immediately upon construction, running the callable passed to its constructor concurrently with the thread that created it.

questionText: What is the difference between calling join() and detach() on a std::thread?
options: They behave identically; both simply stop the thread immediately
join() blocks the calling thread until the thread finishes execution, while detach() lets the thread run independently in the background, with the std::thread object no longer able to be joined
detach() blocks until completion, while join() runs the thread in the background
join() can only be called once per program, while detach() can be called multiple times
explanation: join() waits for the thread to complete before continuing, while detach() separates the std::thread object from the actual thread of execution, allowing it to continue running independently and cleanup automatically when it finishes.

questionText: What is std::mutex used for in concurrent C++ programs?
options: To speed up single-threaded code
To provide mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one thread can hold the lock (and therefore access a protected shared resource) at a time
To automatically parallelize a loop across multiple threads
To convert blocking calls into non-blocking ones
explanation: std::mutex provides a lock that only one thread can hold at a time; a thread calling lock() blocks until it acquires the mutex, protecting shared data from concurrent, unsynchronized access by multiple threads.

questionText: Why is std::lock_guard preferred over manually calling mutex.lock() and mutex.unlock()?
options: It makes the mutex lock faster to acquire
It follows RAII, automatically unlocking the mutex when the lock_guard goes out of scope, even if an exception is thrown, preventing forgotten or skipped unlocks
It allows the same mutex to be locked recursively without restriction
It removes the need for a mutex altogether
explanation: std::lock_guard locks the mutex in its constructor and unlocks it in its destructor, so the mutex is guaranteed to be released when the guard goes out of scope, including during stack unwinding from an exception.

questionText: What extra flexibility does std::unique_lock offer compared to std::lock_guard?
options: None; they are functionally identical in every way
std::unique_lock supports deferred locking, manual unlock/relock, timed locking, and transfer of ownership, whereas std::lock_guard only locks on construction and unlocks on destruction
std::unique_lock can only be used with recursive_mutex
std::unique_lock does not release the mutex automatically at all
explanation: std::unique_lock is a more flexible RAII lock wrapper: it supports deferring the lock, unlocking early and relocking, timed/try locks, and can be moved, at the cost of slightly more overhead than lock_guard.

questionText: What does std::recursive_mutex allow that a plain std::mutex does not?
options: It allows multiple different threads to hold the lock simultaneously
It allows the same thread that already holds the lock to lock it again (recursively) without deadlocking, as long as it unlocks it the same number of times
It automatically prevents deadlocks between different threads
It removes the need for locking altogether in recursive functions
explanation: std::recursive_mutex can be locked multiple times by the same thread without blocking that thread, useful when a locked function calls another function that also needs the same lock, as long as unlock() is called a matching number of times.

questionText: What is a deadlock in concurrent programming?
options: A situation where a thread runs faster than expected
A situation where two or more threads are each waiting for a resource held by another, so none of them can ever proceed
A crash caused by accessing invalid memory
A compiler error that occurs when using multiple mutexes
explanation: A deadlock occurs when threads form a cycle of waiting - e.g. thread A holds mutex 1 and waits for mutex 2, while thread B holds mutex 2 and waits for mutex 1 - so neither can make progress.

questionText: What is a data race in C++, and why is it undefined behavior?
options: Any situation where two threads read the same variable at the same time

When two or more threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one of them writing, without any synchronization to order the accesses, which the standard defines as undefined behavior
A performance issue that only slows down the program, with no correctness impact
A situation that can only occur with global variables, never with local ones
explanation: A data race happens when unsynchronized concurrent accesses to the same memory location include at least one write; the C++ standard specifies this as undefined behavior, which can manifest as corrupted data or worse.

questionText: What does std::atomic, introduced in C++11, provide?
options: A way to make an entire function execute as a single transaction
Types whose operations (like increment, load, store) are guaranteed to be indivisible and free of data races when accessed concurrently from multiple threads, without needing an explicit mutex
A container for storing atomic weights and chemical data
A replacement for all uses of std::thread
explanation: std::atomic<T> wraps a value so that operations on it (like fetch_add, load, store, compare_exchange) are indivisible and safe under concurrent access, often implemented with lock-free hardware instructions.

questionText: What does std::condition_variable, introduced in C++11, allow threads to do?
options: It lets a thread permanently pause another thread from outside
It allows a thread to block (wait) until notified by another thread that some condition may have changed, typically used together with a mutex to avoid busy-waiting
It replaces the need for mutexes when sharing data between threads
It converts a synchronous function into an asynchronous one automatically
explanation: std::condition_variable lets a thread wait efficiently (without busy-looping) until another thread calls notify_one()/notify_all() after changing some shared state, typically checked under a std::unique_lock.

questionText: What does std::async, introduced in C++11, do?
options: It immediately blocks the calling thread until the given function finishes
It runs a callable, potentially asynchronously on a separate thread (or lazily on demand), and returns a std::future through which the result can later be retrieved
It permanently detaches a thread with no way to retrieve a result
It is a synonym for std::thread with no differences
explanation: std::async(func, args...) launches func (possibly on a new thread, depending on the launch policy) and returns a std::future that will hold the result once the computation completes, retrievable via future.get().

questionText: What does std::future represent in C++11's concurrency support?
options: A guaranteed prediction of a program's runtime behavior
A handle to a result that will become available at some point, typically produced by std::async, std::promise, or std::packaged_task, retrieved by calling get() (which blocks until ready)
A container that stores multiple asynchronous results
A type used only for scheduling timers
explanation: A std::future represents a not-yet-available result of an asynchronous operation. Calling get() blocks until the result is ready and returns it (or rethrows an exception if the operation failed).

questionText: What is std::promise used for, in relation to std::future?
options: It is a synonym for std::future with no real difference

A std::promise lets one thread set a value (or exception) that becomes available through an associated std::future obtained from that promise, enabling manual producer/consumer communication between threads
It automatically retries a failed asynchronous operation
It is used only for guaranteeing memory allocation will succeed
explanation: std::promise<T> lets a producer thread call set_value() (or set_exception()) to deliver a result, which becomes retrievable through the std::future<T> obtained via promise.get_future(), used by a consumer thread.

questionText: What does std::packaged_task, introduced in C++11, do?
options: It compresses a task's data to reduce memory usage
It wraps a callable so that its result (or exception) is stored and made available through an associated std::future, decoupling task creation from the decision of when and where it runs
It automatically schedules a task to run at a specific time
It is only usable with lambda expressions, not regular functions
explanation: std::packaged_task wraps a callable and connects it to a std::future; invoking the packaged_task runs the callable and stores its result for retrieval via the future, useful for queuing tasks to run on a thread pool.

questionText: How can std::call_once, introduced in C++11, be used to implement a thread-safe singleton or one-time initialization?
options: It cannot be used for this purpose; a mutex must always be used manually instead
std::call_once, together with a std::once_flag, guarantees that a given callable runs exactly once across all threads, even if multiple threads call it concurrently
It runs a callable once per thread, so it executes multiple times across a multi-threaded program
It is a synonym for std::atomic with no special initialization semantics
explanation: std::call_once(flag, func) ensures func runs exactly once total, even if many threads call std::call_once with the same std::once_flag concurrently, making it a clean way to implement thread-safe lazy initialization.

questionText: What is std::jthread, introduced in C++20, and how does it improve on std::thread?
options: It is identical to std::thread with a different name
It automatically joins in its destructor if still joinable, and supports cooperative cancellation via an associated std::stop_token, reducing the risk of forgetting to call join()
It can only run lambdas, not free functions
It removes the need for any synchronization primitives
explanation: std::jthread ('joining thread') automatically calls join() in its destructor if the thread is still joinable, and integrates a std::stop_token/std::stop_source mechanism for requesting cooperative cancellation.

questionText: What do std::latch and std::barrier, introduced in C++20, provide?
options: They are synonyms for std::mutex with different names

They are synchronization primitives that let a group of threads wait until a certain number of operations complete; a latch is single-use, while a barrier can be reused across multiple synchronization phases
They replace std::atomic entirely
They are used only for file I/O synchronization
explanation: std::latch is a single-use countdown synchronization point that threads can wait on until the count reaches zero, while std::barrier is reusable, letting a fixed group of threads repeatedly synchronize at multiple points in their execution.

questionText: What is 'false sharing' in the context of multithreaded performance?
options: A bug where two threads read the same incorrect value

A performance problem where independent variables used by different threads happen to sit on the same CPU cache line, causing unnecessary cache invalidation traffic between cores even though there is no actual data race
A synonym for a data race that always produces incorrect results
An issue that only affects single-threaded programs
explanation: False sharing occurs when logically independent variables accessed by different threads happen to reside on the same cache line; writes by one thread invalidate the cache line for others, hurting performance despite there being no logical data race.

questionText: What is a race condition, and how does it differ from a data race?
options: They are exactly the same thing with no distinction

A race condition is a broader term for when the correctness of a program depends on the relative timing of events, while a data race specifically refers to unsynchronized concurrent access to the same memory with at least one writer
A race condition can only happen in single-threaded programs
A data race is always safe as long as no exception is thrown
explanation: A race condition is a general timing-dependent correctness bug (which may or may not involve undefined behavior), while a data race is the specific, formally-defined case of unsynchronized concurrent memory access with a write, which the C++ standard deems undefined behavior.

questionText: What does memory ordering (e.g. std::memory_order_relaxed vs std::memory_order_seq_cst) control when used with std::atomic operations?
options: How much memory an atomic variable occupies

How operations on atomics are allowed to be reordered relative to other memory operations, and what visibility guarantees other threads have about the order of writes, trading strictness for performance
The physical memory address where the atomic variable is stored
Whether an atomic variable is stored on the stack or the heap
explanation: Memory order parameters control the compiler/CPU's freedom to reorder memory operations around an atomic operation and what other threads are guaranteed to observe; std::memory_order_seq_cst is the strictest default, while relaxed orderings allow more reordering for performance in careful lock-free code.

questionText: What does std::chrono::duration, from the <chrono> header introduced in C++11, represent?
options: A specific point in calendar time, like a date
A span of time expressed as a count of a given tick period (e.g. std::chrono::seconds, std::chrono::milliseconds), used for measuring or specifying time intervals
A timer that automatically triggers a callback
A synonym for time_t from the C standard library
explanation: std::chrono::duration<Rep, Period> represents a length of time as a count of ticks of a given period, e.g. std::chrono::milliseconds(500) represents 500 milliseconds, and durations of different units can be converted between each other.

questionText: What is the difference between std::chrono::system_clock and std::chrono::steady_clock?
options: They are identical and interchangeable in all situations

system_clock represents wall-clock (calendar) time and can jump backward or forward (e.g. due to NTP sync), while steady_clock never goes backward, making it suitable for measuring elapsed time/durations
steady_clock is used only for calendar dates, while system_clock is used only for timers
system_clock is more precise than steady_clock in every implementation
explanation: system_clock reflects real-world wall-clock time and can be adjusted (e.g. by NTP), so it can jump. steady_clock is monotonic and guaranteed never to go backward, making it the right choice for measuring elapsed durations.

questionText: What do std::cin and std::cout, from <iostream>, represent?
options: Functions for reading and writing files on disk
Global stream objects representing standard input and standard output, used with the >> and << operators to read from the console and write formatted text to it
Classes that must be instantiated manually before use
Deprecated C-style I/O functions replaced by printf and scanf
explanation: std::cin and std::cout are predefined global stream objects for standard input and output; >> extracts data from cin into variables, and << inserts data into cout to be printed to the console.

questionText: What do stream manipulators like std::setw and std::setprecision, from <iomanip>, do?
options: They permanently change a value's underlying data type
They control how subsequent output is formatted, such as std::setw(10) setting a minimum field width and std::setprecision(2) controlling the number of digits shown for floating-point values
They validate user input for errors
They can only be used with std::cin, not std::cout
explanation: Manipulators like std::setw(n), std::setprecision(n), and std::fixed adjust how values are formatted when inserted into a stream, controlling things like field width, decimal precision, and number formatting.

questionText: What are std::ifstream and std::ofstream, from <fstream>, used for?
options: For formatting numbers with fixed precision
For reading from files (ifstream) and writing to files (ofstream) using the same stream-based interface (>> and <<) as std::cin and std::cout
For creating in-memory-only streams with no file access
For managing network sockets
explanation: std::ifstream (input file stream) and std::ofstream (output file stream) let you read from and write to files using the familiar >> and << stream operators, treating file I/O consistently with console I/O.

questionText: What is std::stringstream, from <sstream>, commonly used for?
options: For compressing strings to save memory
For treating a std::string as an in-memory stream, useful for parsing values out of a string or building up a string incrementally using << and >>
For encrypting string data
For comparing two strings for equality
explanation: std::stringstream lets you use stream operators (<<, >>) on an in-memory string buffer, which is a common technique for parsing tokens out of text or building formatted strings piece by piece.

questionText: What is a common trade-off between using printf-style functions from <cstdio> versus iostream for output?
options: printf is type-safe, while iostream is not

printf-style functions can be more concise for complex formatting but are not type-safe (mismatched format specifiers cause undefined behavior), while iostream is type-safe but historically more verbose for complex formatting
There is no difference between them at all
iostream cannot be used to print to the console, only to files
explanation: printf-family functions use format strings checked (if at all) only by compiler extensions, so a mismatched %d/%s is undefined behavior, whereas iostream's << operator is type-safe at compile time, though traditionally more verbose for complex number formatting.

questionText: What kinds of functions does the <cmath> header provide?
options: String manipulation functions like strlen and strcpy
Mathematical functions such as sqrt, pow, sin, cos, floor, and ceil for floating-point computations
Functions for managing dynamic memory allocation
Functions exclusively for random number generation
explanation: <cmath> provides common mathematical functions like std::sqrt, std::pow, std::sin, std::cos, std::floor, and std::ceil, operating on floating-point types.

questionText: Why are C-string functions from <cstring>, like strcpy, considered risky?
options: They are risky because they run too slowly compared to std::string

Functions like strcpy do not check the destination buffer's size, so copying a string longer than the buffer causes a buffer overflow, a classic source of memory corruption and security vulnerabilities
They can only operate on wide character strings, not regular char arrays
They automatically throw exceptions on any error, making them hard to use
explanation: strcpy and similar functions blindly copy until a null terminator is found, with no bounds checking, so an oversized source string can overflow the destination buffer, corrupting memory - a common source of security vulnerabilities.

questionText: What kinds of tools does the <algorithm> header provide?
options: Only sorting algorithms and nothing else
A broad collection of generic algorithms that operate on iterator ranges, such as sort, find, count, transform, reverse, and copy, working across many different container types
Only mathematical algorithms for numeric computation
Networking and file transfer algorithms
explanation: <algorithm> provides generic, container-agnostic algorithms (sort, find, count, transform, reverse, copy, and many more) that operate on iterator ranges, working uniformly across vectors, lists, arrays, and other containers.

questionText: What does the <regex> library, standardized in C++11, provide?
options: A way to compress and decompress text data
Support for regular expressions, allowing pattern matching and searching/replacing within strings using std::regex, std::regex_match, and std::regex_search
A replacement for std::string with automatic validation
A tool exclusively for parsing XML and JSON
explanation: <regex> brings regular expression support to the standard library, with std::regex representing a compiled pattern and functions like std::regex_search/std::regex_match/std::regex_replace for using it against strings.

questionText: Why is the <random> library, introduced in C++11, generally preferred over the old C rand() function?
options: rand() is faster and produces higher-quality randomness in every case

<random> separates the random number engine (e.g. std::mt19937) from the distribution (e.g. std::uniform_int_distribution), providing better statistical quality and more control than rand()'s single global generator
rand() cannot generate numbers within a specific range at all
<random> can only generate floating-point numbers, not integers
explanation: <random> cleanly separates the pseudo-random engine (like std::mt19937) from how numbers are distributed (like std::uniform_int_distribution), offering better statistical properties and more control than rand(), which is a single, often low-quality, global generator.

questionText: What does the <filesystem> library, standardized in C++17, provide?
options: A way to compress files automatically

A portable API for working with file system paths and operations, such as checking if a file exists, iterating a directory, and creating or removing files/directories, via std::filesystem::path and related functions
A replacement for std::fstream that cannot read file contents
A tool exclusively for network file transfers
explanation: <filesystem> (std::filesystem) offers a portable way to manipulate paths and query/modify the file system, e.g. std::filesystem::exists(), directory_iterator, create_directory(), and remove(), without relying on platform-specific APIs.

questionText: What does the <stdexcept> header provide, and how are its exception types typically organized?
options: A single generic exception type used for all error cases
A hierarchy of standard exception classes such as std::logic_error and std::runtime_error (with further subclasses like std::out_of_range and std::invalid_argument), all deriving from std::exception
Only exceptions related to file input/output errors
A macro-based error handling system that does not use C++ exceptions at all
explanation: <stdexcept> defines a hierarchy rooted at std::exception, split broadly into std::logic_error (e.g. std::out_of_range, std::invalid_argument) for programming errors and std::runtime_error (e.g. std::overflow_error) for runtime conditions.

questionText: What kinds of tools does the <numeric> header provide, distinct from <algorithm>?
options: String formatting utilities
Numeric algorithms for combining ranges of values, such as std::accumulate for folding/summing a range, std::inner_product, and std::iota for filling a range with sequentially increasing values
Only trigonometric functions like sin and cos
Random number generation engines
explanation: <numeric> focuses on numeric operations over ranges, including std::accumulate (fold/sum), std::inner_product, std::iota (fills a range with increasing values starting from a given value), and related algorithms like std::gcd.

questionText: What common utilities does the <utility> header provide?
options: Only mathematical constants like pi
General-purpose utilities including std::pair, std::swap, std::move, and std::forward, which are foundational tools used throughout the standard library
Only file path manipulation functions
Multithreading primitives like mutexes
explanation: <utility> is a small but foundational header providing std::pair, std::swap, and the C++11 additions std::move and std::forward, which are used extensively throughout the rest of the standard library.

questionText: Which header declares the smart pointer types std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, and std::weak_ptr?
options: <utility>
<memory>
<pointer>
<smart_ptr>
explanation: The <memory> header declares std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, std::weak_ptr, std::make_unique, std::make_shared, and other memory-management utilities.

questionText: What does the <thread> header, introduced in C++11, declare?
options: Only mutex and lock types
The std::thread class itself, along with the std::this_thread namespace containing functions like sleep_for, sleep_until, and get_id
Only atomic types like std::atomic<int>
File I/O streams for reading thread dumps
explanation: <thread> declares std::thread for creating and managing threads, plus the std::this_thread namespace with utilities such as std::this_thread::sleep_for and std::this_thread::get_id.

questionText: What does the assert macro, from <cassert>, do?
options: It always terminates the program regardless of build configuration
It checks a condition at runtime and, if false, prints diagnostic information and aborts the program, but is typically compiled out entirely in release builds when NDEBUG is defined
It logs a warning to a file without stopping execution
It is a compile-time check identical to static_assert
explanation: assert(condition) checks a runtime condition and calls std::abort with diagnostic info if it is false, but including the NDEBUG macro during compilation strips out all assert checks, so it should not be relied on for release-build error handling.

questionText: What does the <cstdint> header, standardized in C++11 (based on C99), provide?
options: String conversion functions like stoi and to_string
Fixed-width integer types such as int32_t, uint64_t, and int8_t, whose exact bit width is guaranteed, unlike int or long whose sizes can vary across platforms
Only floating-point types with guaranteed precision
Container types for storing large integers of arbitrary precision
explanation: <cstdint> defines fixed-width integer types like int8_t, uint32_t, and int64_t with a guaranteed exact bit width, which is important for portable code where the size of int or long could otherwise vary by platform.
